headline: Massachusetts, Connecticut AGs seek privacy safeguards as Character.AI enters bankruptcy sale
dek: A multistate filing asks the bankruptcy court to protect sensitive chats and children’s data if the chatbot company’s assets are sold.
body: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell and Connecticut Attorney General William Tong have joined a multistate effort to protect users’ private information as Character Technologies, the company behind Character.AI, moves through a court-supervised bankruptcy sale. The states’ notice, filed in the company’s Chapter 11 proceedings on Oct. 14, raises concerns about the platform’s safety practices and asks that any sale of the business or its assets include protections for children and other consumers, according to the [Massachusetts attorney general’s office](https://www.mass.gov/news/ag-campbell-seeks-consumer-protections-in-characterai-bankruptcy).

Character.AI is an online service where people converse with artificial-intelligence characters designed to imitate human relationships. The characters can be fictional or based on celebrities and children’s media, while some present themselves as psychologists, therapists or doctors. The state attorneys general said those interactions have generated sensitive records, including private conversations about mental health, relationships and emotional distress. Their concern is not limited to the continued operation of the app; it also reaches what could happen to that information if ownership changes.

The filing comes two days after Character.AI said it had voluntarily entered Chapter 11 to pursue a sale of all or substantially all of its assets. In its [company update](https://blog.character.ai/an-update-on-character-ai/), Character.AI said the platform remains available, subscriptions remain active and the sale process could finish by late November or early December. The company also said the service could be wound down if the court-supervised process does not produce an actionable proposal to keep it operating.

All six New England states are represented in the coalition: Massachusetts, Connecticut, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. The broader list released by Connecticut also includes New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, along with attorneys general from several other states and territories. That regional participation matters because the dispute is moving beyond a single company’s privacy policy and into a federal bankruptcy process that can determine how a digital platform, its contracts and its data are handled.

Connecticut’s filing says several states began investigating Character.AI after a 2024 wrongful-death lawsuit alleged that one of the company’s chatbots fostered an emotionally and sexually exploitative relationship with a child, reinforced suicidal thoughts and contributed to the child’s death. Those are allegations, not findings in the bankruptcy case. Connecticut officials said their investigation identified potential consumer-protection and privacy violations, while the states reserved the right to challenge a proposed sale or bankruptcy plan and to seek additional safeguards.

The attorneys general are also questioning the durability of protections Character.AI has recently put in place for minors. Tong’s office said the restrictions are voluntary, incomplete and potentially subject to circumvention or reversal by a future purchaser. The states’ filing therefore seeks protections that would travel with the company through the sale, rather than relying only on policies that a new owner could later change. The public materials do not yet establish what specific buyer, if any, would take over the full platform or what final treatment the court would approve for user data.

Character.AI says its privacy and security practices have not changed during the case. The company’s user guidance says people can delete their accounts or export their data through the app or website, but that statement is the company’s current position, not a ruling on how a bankruptcy sale must be structured. Users who are deciding what to do with their accounts should distinguish between what the company promises now and what a court-approved transaction may require later.

The financial pressure behind the filing adds another layer to the regional consumer-protection debate. [TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/13/just-5-years-in-interactive-chatbot-platform-character-ai-files-for-bankruptcy/) that a court document placed Character.AI’s assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million and that the company had agreed to sell some assets to Disney for $20 million, along with a non-exclusive perpetual technology license. That reported transaction is not the same as a completed sale of the entire platform, and TechCrunch said the company had not identified a buyer for all of its assets.

The next milestones are procedural: the bankruptcy court will consider the sale process and any proposed plan, while the state attorneys general decide whether the terms adequately protect consumers. For Massachusetts and Connecticut residents, the case creates a live test of how state privacy and child-safety concerns can be carried into federal bankruptcy proceedings. It also leaves a central question unresolved: whether a future owner can continue the service without turning deeply personal chatbot conversations into an asset whose protections depend on a new company’s policy.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts, Connecticut AGs Seek Character.AI Privacy Safeguards
seoDescription: Massachusetts and Connecticut joined a multistate filing seeking privacy and child-safety protections in Character.AI’s Chapter 11 sale.
